rivers: Dhopajan, Fazilpur and Dowarabazar sand-mixed stone quarries
records.summary: A notification dated 16 November, signed by Bureau of Mineral Development (BMD) Director General Mohammad Robiul Faysal, ordered khas collection to begin at gazetted sand-mixed stone quarries in Sadar, Bishwambharpur, Tahirpur and Dowarabazar upazilas of Sunamganj district. The article's headline and listing name three quarries: Dhopajan (182 hectares, Sadar and Bishwambharpur), Fazilpur (121.49 hectares, Tahirpur) and an unnamed gazetted quarry in Dowarabazar (45.93 hectares). The intro says four quarries; the report names no river. The notification says the government is losing large revenue because leasing has long been suspended. It says the quarries are remote and hard to reach, so regular mobile courts could not stop illegal extraction of stone and sand-mixed stone. Under Rule 95 of the Mines and Minerals Rules 2012, if no lease is granted, money can be collected through the district commissioner as khas land until leasing is completed. Extraction must be wholly by traditional methods, with no excavator, dredger or bomb machine. High Court status quo, stay or injunction orders must be considered first. Collection must be monitored regularly and the money deposited in a designated BMD code.

records.title: Armed terror, nighttime sand looting grip Meghna riverbanks in Nabinagar
records.titleEn: Armed terror, nighttime sand looting grip Meghna riverbanks in Nabinagar
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's account citing residents (Abdul Awal), the paper's investigations, and statements by the Deputy Commissioner and Police Superintendent
records.location: Dharabhanga, Charlapang, Marichakandi, Kanaigar and Shantinagar villages, Nabinagar Upazila, Brahmanbaria
records.summary: Daily Country Today reported that villages along the Meghna River in Nabinagar Upazila, Brahmanbaria, face an armed syndicate conducting illegal sand mining every night. Over 25 dredgers, operated by a cross-district syndicate from Raipura Upazila, Narsingdi, reportedly move close to homes after dark, extracting 40 to 50 million cubic feet of sand daily, worth several crores of taka. The report says the operation has already swallowed homes and cropland, and that Dharabhanga, Charlapang, Marichakandi, Kanaigar and Shantinagar villages face imminent collapse. Locals said hired armed cadres patrol the banks at night, with a surge in drug trafficking and intimidation. Dharabhanga resident Abdul Awal said residents spend sleepless nights fearing the dredgers and embankment collapse. The paper's investigations link the syndicate to known criminals and politically connected figures; in Nabinagar and Bancharampur it allegedly includes Monak Dakat, his sons Suman and Roman, and Md. Mahabubul Alam Qayyum, locally identified as a nephew of the Brahmanbaria-6 MP. The Raipura faction is reportedly led by Harun, Obaidullah, Nayan Sheikh and local Jubo Dal leader Qayyum Mia. Despite month-long complaints, the lack of visible intervention has sparked suspicion of administrative complicity. Deputy Commissioner Md. Abu Sayeed said preparations are underway to form a joint task force. Police Superintendent Md. Jalal Uddin Fahim cited manpower shortages for the lack of night patrols but pledged to reinforce the Salimganj police outpost and launch a coordinated crackdown with Narsingdi police soon.

Locals and administration sources alleged he used influence to win a contract to supply sand for an RCC road from Panchabati graveyard to Hamchhadi, then occupied residents' land after claiming to buy it at nominal prices. Local journalists alleged he mistreated and threatened them when they went to report. Anonymous locals made further allegations, whose truth the report says could not be independently confirmed. records.titleEn: Allegation of sand and homestead soil being lifted from Surma River with dredger in Chhatak
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's three-day site visit; resident statements; police outpost in-charge quoted; UNO unreachable
records.location: Bausa-Keshabpur village, Chhatak Sadar union, Chhatak upazila, Sunamganj; also Chairchira, Ranamangal and Pratappur villages
records.summary: Residents of Chhatak, Sunamganj alleged that an influential group is illegally using dredger machines to lift sand and homestead soil (bhitemati) from the Surma River. A three-day site visit (Saturday, Sunday, Monday) found dredgers lifting sand and soil and loading it onto boats in the Surma near Bausa-Keshabpur village, Chhatak Sadar union. Residents claimed that for the past week the same day-and-night extraction has also been going on near Chairchira, Ranamangal and Pratappur villages. They said the people behind it are unclear, though workers operate openly, and they suspect the material may be supplied to the under-construction Chhatak-Gobindaganj road. Residents fear harm to river flow, environment, banks and settlements. They said erosion of the Surma has already swallowed farmland, mosques, graveyards and other structures in Mallikpur, Machhukhali, Andharigaon and Bausa-Keshabpur on the south bank and Lakshibaur and Betura on the north bank, and damaged government earthen and paved roads, with erosion continuing. One south-bank resident said land erosion in Bausa-Keshabpur alone created a char of about 1,100 acres on the opposite bank. Locals also alleged that an influential group uses political identity to manage the administration; no response from those concerned was obtained. Chhatak river police outpost in-charge Arabindu Roy said he was unaware of the week-long open dredging. Residents demanded a quick investigation. Chhatak Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mohi Uddin did not answer repeated phone calls.

records.title: ​যমুনার চরে বালু লুট, হুমকিতে কৃষকের জীবিকা
records.titleEn: Sand looted from Jamuna char, farmers' livelihoods under threat
records.dateEvidence: Reporter site visit; statements from residents, a local Juba Dal official, workers, lessee Haji Abdus Sattar, and the Assistant Commissioner (Land); upazila administration sources on lease coverage.
records.location: Motiyarpur area, Chhonagacha union, Sirajganj Sadar upazila, Sirajganj
rivers: Panchthakuri boat ghat named as stockpile site)
records.summary: Bangla Scoop reported allegations that an influential group is illegally cutting and selling soil and sand from a newly emerged char of the Jamuna at Motiyarpur, Chhonagacha union, Sirajganj Sadar upazila, Sirajganj. Residents alleged that a ring led by local BNP leader Anwar Hossain is operating using the name of Haji Abdus Sattar, lessee of a legal balumahal. Upazila administration sources said three balumahals on the Jamuna in Sirajganj Sadar have been leased (Shimla, GR Para and Chandalboyra mouzas), but none at Motiyarpur, so there is no legal scope to extract there. Residents said that from late night until morning, boats carry soil and sand, which is stockpiled at Panchthakuri boat ghat and sold by truck. The report said farmers who lost homes and land to Jamuna erosion had begun growing groundnut, kalai and chilli on the char, and that the alleged cutting puts the livelihoods of over a hundred (shatadhik) helpless people at risk. Residents alleged that Sabbir Hossain Prantu, employed by Sattar, and Anwar Hossain oversee the boat loads and soil accounts. Residents Motahar Hossain and Jahangir said the boatmen told them they were paying Sattar to cut soil. Farhad Hossain Kalu, a local ward Juba Dal president, alleged that an influential group is extracting sand and soil while evading the administration, and called for an investigation. Some employees involved said they buy soil and sand from Sattar. Sattar denied the allegations, saying only sand from the legal balumahal is meant to be bought for sale and that he has no involvement in cutting the Motiyarpur char. Assistant Commissioner (Land) Abdullah-Hel Mafi said extraction outside leased balumahals is not permitted, that cutting the char is out of the question, that the matter had come to his notice, and that necessary action would be taken. The article gives no volume or fine figures.

records.titleEn: Illegal stone extraction from the Teesta not stopping even after drives
records.dateEvidence: Quotes from residents, a BWDB executive engineer, the Dimla police OC and the Dimla UNO; reporter's account from Lalmonirhat
records.location: Teesta Barrage area, Hatibandha upazila (Lalmonirhat) and Dimla upazila (Nilphamari)
rivers: Teesta river, upstream of the Teesta Barrage
records.summary: NewsBangladesh reported on 15 November 2026 that illegal stone extraction continues on the Teesta river upstream of the Teesta Barrage, in Hatibandha upazila of Lalmonirhat and Dimla upazila of Nilphamari, despite regular drives, cases and arrests. Dredger machines reportedly operate day and night, and stone is piled beside roads and sold openly. Residents alleged that the syndicate is active in at least 12 places, and feared damage to the barrage, more riverbank erosion and worse floods. Resident Rafiqul Islam said stone is taken even very near the barrage; another resident, Abdur Rahman, said the gang often learns of drives in advance and moves its dredgers and boats away. Amitabh Chowdhury, executive engineer of the Dalia Water Development Board (BWDB) office, said stone is being extracted illegally from places downstream of the barrage, security staff were told to stay alert, and the barrage would certainly be at risk if extraction continues. Dimla police OC Ashraful Alam said at least 15 cases were filed over the last ten months and 12 people were arrested; several dredger machines and boats were seized and destroyed. Dimla UNO Md. records.summary: Local residents alleged that sand is being extracted and trafficked from the Dolu, Garurloda and Dhuilya canals in Amtali, Dhuilya and Garurloda villages of Purbachambi area, Aziznagar union, Lama upazila, Bandarban. They claimed more than 30 dredgers have been set up at 12 points within about one kilometre, and that 200 to 300 trucks and dumpers carry the sand away daily, to Lohagara and Satkania upazilas. Residents alleged that four or five organised gangs from neighbouring Lohagara, Chattogram, are involved, parade on motorcycles with local weapons, and are joined by 15 to 20 local people, so that nobody dares protest. On a recent site visit the reporter saw sand piles and dredging. Three dredgers were working on the Dolu canal east of the house of UP member Chhoidur Rahman in Amtali, with trucks loading; two more points lie west of the village near Mohsin Doctor's house and a mosque. Dredgers also operate at the Dolu and Garurloda canal confluence behind Mostafa Nagar, where some locals claimed at least 40 truckloads were removed last Friday morning. Locals claimed 3 to 4 lakh cubic feet of sand is stockpiled at three points near former UP member Haris Mia's house in Garurloda, and that three points operate day and night on the Dhuilya canal. Residents said extraction has grown over two years from two or three points to 12, and many claimed the trade runs by managing the administration. Bank erosion has hit the three canals, and locals claimed houses and farmland have been lost. Residents Abdul Awal and Delwar Hossain said dredger noise disrupts work and sleep. Lama police OC Kaiser Hamid said illegal extraction will not be tolerated and police will assist if the upazila administration acts. records.summary: An editorial in Daily Naya Diganta says indiscriminate illegal stone extraction and looting near the Teesta Barrage is both a misappropriation of state resources and an environmental disaster. Citing a report the paper had published, it says that in the Dalia, Telibazar and Teesta Bazar areas of Dimla upazila, Nilphamari, the single-use auction papers for stone seized by the administration are being reused repeatedly to pass illegally extracted stone off as legal. It asks how such organised fraud is possible where five BGB camps and river police are on guard. A task force run by the upazila administration seized a large quantity of stone and equipment on 14 October; after five lots were sold at open auction on 28 October, the misuse of this 'paper legality' began. Stone is reportedly lifted illegally from the river and mixed into old stockpiles, and even a lot that was never auctioned was reportedly looted at night. The editorial says the extraction threatens the barrage and the river's course, and that unplanned stone and sand removal deepens the riverbed unevenly, which could cause severe bank erosion in the monsoon and structural damage to the barrage. It says local authorities occasionally conduct raids, file cases and make some arrests, but profits outweigh arrests or fines, and flaws in the auction process encourage offenders. It suggests removal deadlines (for example 24 or 48 hours), specific per-consignment papers, digital monitoring of transport, regular joint patrols by BGB, river police and the district administration, and an inquiry into possible negligence or collusion by local guards or others.

records.summary: Complainant Mosaddek Ali, a resident of East Tegharia in Sunamganj town, submitted a written complaint to the Sunamganj Deputy Commissioner and District Magistrate against lessee Md. Nasir Mia, owner of M/s Tahia Stone Crusher and general secretary of Boroddol South union BNP in Tahirpur. The complaint alleges that, in breach of lease conditions, sand is being extracted from the Jadukata-1 and Jadukata-2 mahals, Sunamganj's largest sand mahal, using banned machinery. It alleges that the riverbank and farmland are being cut, a government playground destroyed and a ferry ghat occupied. According to the complaint, the district administration approved extraction from 1 October 2026 to 13 April 2027, but sand is being taken from the riverbank, farmland and other places at Moderagaon outside the lease boundary, using dredgers and machines locally called 'save' or 'bomb machine'. It alleges that the western side of the Moderagaon children's playground is being cut, risking the field's loss. Privately owned three-crop farmland is also allegedly being cut. Hundreds of large sand-laden boats allegedly obstruct movement at the Moderagaon-Ghagra ferry ghat and Gudara ghat. The complaint cites breaches of the Sand Mahal and Soil Management Act 2010 and the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, and seeks cancellation of the lease, criminal action and investigation. Nasir Mia denied the allegations, saying that any bank that was cut was cut just after 5 August 2024, that no bank is being cut now, and that his people are guarding against bank cutting. Additional DC (Revenue) Tapas Shil said he was on leave, was unaware of the complaint and would look into it. Mosaddek Ali said Shil had assured action but none was taken. A Land Ministry order of 22 September permitted extraction until 13 April 2027, at a rate set at 12 percent above the three-year average market value. Revenue for the two mahals was fixed at 42 crore 66 lakh 36 thousand 422 taka, which the district administration collected before handing over possession.

records.title: পাথর কোয়ারি খুললে কর্মসংস্থানের নতুন সম্ভাবনা
records.titleEn: If stone quarries open, new possibilities for employment
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's account citing unnamed concerned parties, the MP, an unnamed source and a trader-worker council convener
records.location: Companiganj, Goainghat, Jaintapur and Kanaighat upazilas, Sylhet; Sylhet and Sunamganj districts
records.summary: The report (Companiganj, 11 November 2026) says the BNP's election pledge of 1 crore (10 million) new jobs could be helped by Sylhet's stone quarries; it names no river, only the quarries of Companiganj, Goainghat, Jaintapur and Kanaighat upazilas, Sylhet. Those concerned claim that legal extraction from seven Sylhet quarries could create jobs for about 10 lakh (1 million) people and reduce import dependence and pressure on foreign-currency reserves. Arif ul Haque Chowdhury, the BNP MP for Sylhet-4 (Companiganj-Goainghat-Jaintapur), had promised extraction from 13 February if he won the 12 February election. Legal complications prevented that, and he has since told journalists extraction will begin this season. Extraction from domestic quarries has been shut for about six years, leaving several lakh people jobless in extraction, transport and crushing work around Companiganj, Goainghat, Jaintapur and Kanaighat. Many markets have closed, many rental flats stand empty, and many traders have gone bankrupt; locals call it a silent famine. Before 2020, quarries in these four upazilas yielded about 50 lakh (5 million) metric tons of stone a year, about 80 percent of national demand. Now about 5,000-6,000 crore taka of stone is imported each year. An unnamed source said Labour and Employment Minister Arif ul Haque Chowdhury has begun efforts to resolve the cases behind the halt. On 7 May a high-level expert committee was formed at a Home Ministry meeting chaired by Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, to review limited re-leasing of Sylhet and Sunamganj quarries. It is led by the Sylhet divisional commissioner and includes the deputy commissioners of both districts, the Department of Environment, the Ministry of Water Resources, the Geological Survey, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, the Ministry of Mineral Resources and both districts' police superintendents. It is reported to have visited the quarries and submitted a report. Abdul Jalil, convener of the Sylhet Divisional Stone-related Traders-Workers Unity Council, said the halt stems from a case filed by the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), and that the quarries have not been leased despite several movements and a transport strike. He said they understand the government is trying to resolve the legal complications through the High Court and re-lease the quarries.

Abdul Quayum Khan said the issue was discussed at the previous day's law and order committee meeting; the administration has no permission to run a mobile team at night, so trackers will be fitted to bulkheads (cargo vessels) during the day and their movements monitored at night before further action.

records.summary: Daily Adin reported on 10 November 2026 that illegal stone extraction from the Teesta River continues in Dimla, Nilphamari, despite repeated administrative drives. The reporter's site visit upstream of the Teesta Barrage, at Telir Bazar, Kisamat Char and Chhotokhata, found workers on more than 400 boats using dredger machines and iron chisels to dig the riverbed for stone. The activity was reported along at least 15 kilometres of the Nilphamari and Lalmonirhat stretch near the Bangladesh-India border. The report says the river's flow and structure have visibly changed, creating several narrow channels, and that erosion has struck at least 20 nearby villages. Eight unions of Dimla and Jaldhaka upazilas are described as erosion-affected. The barrage, the flood control embankment, farmland and riverside communities are said to be threatened. At least 10 residents of Kisamat Char, including Arif Hossain and Anwar Ali, said their village was lost over the past two years, and that several thousand people sheltered beside the embankment road. Residents said stone has been extracted daily from dawn to midnight for two years and carried by truck along the embankment road. They alleged that extractors post lookouts on access roads who warn of administration vehicles, so workers and equipment are moved before raids. Local sources said each truck carries about 500 to 700 cubic feet of stone and sells for 50,000 to 80,000 taka, supplied to construction work in various districts. Tepakhoribari union chairman Rabiul Islam Shahin said he was attacked by extractors when trying to stop the extraction and alleged an attempt to kill him. He said the case he filed is pending in court. Dimla police OC Ashraful Alam said at least 15 cases have been filed against illegal stone traders and at least 12 people arrested. An unnamed law enforcement member said many arrestees get bail quickly and return to extraction. Dalia Water Development Board executive engineer Amitabh Chowdhury said cutting the riverbed destroys its natural depth and structure and may worsen erosion. Tista Bachao Nadi Bachao Andolan central member Sohel Hasan said raids alone cannot solve the problem and the whole network must be identified. Dimla UNO Imranuzzaman said the administration acts on information, seizing equipment, filing cases and making arrests, but extractors resume after raids because the area is remote.

records.title: Who Is Behind the Looting of Stones from the Teesta River?
records.titleEn: Who Is Behind the Looting of Stones from the Teesta River?
records.dateEvidence: Upazila administration records, reporter field visit, resident and journalist statements, officials quoted, secretly recorded video reported by Ajker Patrika
records.location: Kisamat Char, Barnir Ghat, Khagar Char, Chhotokhata, Char Kharibari, Telir Bazar, Dimla and Jaldhaka upazilas, Nilphamari (also Lalmonirhat border section)
rivers: Teesta River (upstream of the Teesta Barrage)
records.summary: The report says illegal sand and stone extraction continues on the Teesta River in Nilphamari despite raids, cases, seizures and arrests, putting the Teesta Barrage and flood-control embankments at serious risk. Upazila administration records show at least 20 operations between June last year and October this year, with seizure and destruction of three stone-carrying tractors, one truck, five crusher machines, dredgers, shallow-engine boats, thousands of feet of pipes and more than 29,000 cubic feet of stones; twelve people were arrested. Hotspots include Barnir Ghat upstream of the barrage, reserved Kisamat Char (Jhar Singhereshwar and Thangjhara BGB camp areas), Khagar Char, Chhotokhata and Char Kharibari, where operations were conducted at least five times. Extraction reportedly resumes within days or weeks. A field visit found eight unions in Dimla and Jaldhaka upazilas affected by erosion. At Telir Bazar, Kisamat Char and Chhotokhata, workers were seen using dredgers on more than 400 boats and iron chisels; the activity stretches across at least 15 kilometres along the Nilphamari and Lalmonirhat border sections, has created several narrow channels, and erosion has emerged in at least 20 nearby villages. Residents of Kisamat Char, including Arif Hossain, Anwar Ali and at least eight other residents, said the village was washed away over two years and several thousand people sheltered along the embankment road; they said extraction runs daily from early morning to midnight. Locals alleged lookouts warn extractors of raids. Local sources said each truck carries about 500 to 700 cubic feet of stones, sold for Tk50,000 to Tk80,000 per truck. Local journalist Rezwan Islam said more than 400 boats are used for extraction every day despite a BGB camp and river police in the area, and alleged that river police are involved, leak raid plans and take bribes. Ajker Patrika reported a secretly recorded video in which two ASIs of Dalia River Police Outpost, Swapan and Shamim, admitted collecting regular payments from each boat. Attacks on officials, journalists and local representatives were reported, including on an Independent Television team (case against 20 to 25 people, no arrests, per the correspondent) and on Teparkharibari UP chairman Rabiul Islam Shahin. Residents alleged a group of 20 to 30 people, led by trader Ziarul Islam, is involved; trader Jahangir Alam denied involvement. Dimla OC Ashraful Alam said at least 15 cases were filed and at least 12 people arrested. An anonymous law enforcement member said arrestees quickly get bail and return. Water Development Board engineer Amitabha Chowdhury warned of damaged river depth and worse erosion. UNO Imranuzzaman said areas are hard to access, so extraction resumes after operations. State Minister Farhad Hossain Azad said strict instructions would be given to both districts' administrations.

A reporter visiting on Friday (6 November) saw dredging under way. Locals alleged that an influential man, Nazrul Molla, operates the dredger, sells the soil elsewhere and uses it to fill several plots, despite a permit condition forbidding sale of soil cut by dredging. According to the permit, signed on 10 September 2026 by the then Upazila Executive Officer Setu Kumar Barua, dredging was allowed for just three days. Residents fear loss of soil fertility and harm to agriculture and the environment. Nazrul Molla said agriculture office officials had inspected the site and that journalists and police knew about it. Sub-assistant agriculture officer Sajib Sarkar said the land was a flat crop field, never used for fish farming, and that he did not know who gave permission. Upazila fisheries officer Belayet Hossain said soil should not have been cut for so long as only three days' permission was taken. Assistant Commissioner (Land) Anisur Rahman could not be reached by phone. Current UNO Mehedi Hasan (Manik) said he was looking into how dredging continued so long. Locals demanded an immediate halt, an investigation and legal action.

records.summary: A Mymensingh-datelined report (by Nihar Ranjan Kundu, published 5 November 2026) alleges that a group is continuously extracting sand illegally from the Brahmaputra erosion area at Bottola, Uchakhila union (near Chorrammohan village), Ishwarganj upazila, Mymensingh. It says they use dredger machines loading cargo vessels and boats, and boring in residential areas, in defiance of High Court Writ Petition No. 166 of 2020. The report says the High Court ordered the Bottola sandghat closed on 22 June 2020 on an application by Rafiqul Islam, son of Abdul Kadir of Ujancharan para. It alleges that, after the change of power, Rafiqul himself is leading the extraction with several named associates. Several local people said the extraction runs from early evening through the night, using dredgers and large cargo vessels. They said the upazila administration stayed silent after being informed, and argued this proves the authorities are involved. Residents alleged that the administration has been "managed" and that the government geo-bag embankment protecting homes from river erosion, as well as farmland and the environment, is under threat. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Azim Uddin said Mymensingh district currently has no sand mahal plots and that quick action would be taken against illegal extraction. After a written complaint by Mizan on behalf of locals, he reportedly instructed the upazila executive officer, who directed the assistant commissioner (land) to stop the extraction. The UNO also advised regular cases against violators if it continued. Locals demanded exemplary punishment for Rafiqul Islam. The report also says no sand mahal was declared in Ishwarganj or Mymensingh district in the current fiscal year. The named individuals' responses are not given.

records.summary: Bhorer Kagoj's Sherpur correspondent reported allegations of illegal hill cutting and stone and sand extraction from hills, rivers and streams in the border Garo hills of Jhenaigati upazila, Sherpur. According to local sources, extraction is taking place in areas along the Kalghosha river in Kangsha union, including Gandhigaon, Darbeshtala, Halchati, Malitila, Bakakura, Gajni and Chhoto Gajni, and in reserved forest. Residents alleged an organised syndicate has long been doing this openly and looting natural resources worth lakhs of taka every day. More than a hundred workers are alleged to be cutting hills and collecting stone and sand with shovels and spades. The material is reportedly stockpiled in the forest, carried by basket and on heads, then transported after 12 midnight by horse cart, van, trolley, Mahindra and truck to the upazila and district town. Locals claimed this transport runs from 12 midnight to 8 am daily. Environmentally conscious people said continued extraction would change the hill landforms, disrupt stream and river flow, destroy wildlife habitat and make the Garo hills lose their appeal to tourists. The report describes the Gajni Obokash recreation centre, set up in 1993, as a major attraction of the Garo hills and a yearly revenue source for the government, without giving a figure. It says that mobile courts have at times seized sand-carrying vehicles, fined and jailed people, yet extraction has allegedly not stopped. On the night of 3 June, after four sand-laden Mahindra vehicles were seized, extractors allegedly attacked and injured Gajni forest beat officer Md. Salehin Newaz and a forest guard named Ziaur Rahman; locals allege forest department activity has since declined. Rangtia forest range officer Md. Habibullah declined to comment. Salehin Newaz said river sand falls under the district administration, which must act. Sherpur Deputy Commissioner Farida Yasmin said she had directed the upazila executive officer (UNO) to take necessary action. Locals demanded regular drives, identification and prosecution of extractors, and stronger monitoring of the reserved forest.

records.titleEn: Sand extraction at Parki in Chattogram, Karnaphuli Tunnel service area at risk of erosion
records.dateEvidence: Reporter site visits on Saturday and Monday; statements from residents, a Premier supervisor and engineer, and the Anwara assistant commissioner (land)
records.location: Parki sea beach, Barashat union, Anwara upazila, Chattogram
rivers: Karnaphuli River near Parki beach and Karnaphuli Tunnel service area
records.summary: Ajker Patrika reported allegations that sand is being extracted with a dredger and booster machines from the Karnaphuli River adjacent to Parki sea beach in Anwara upazila, Chattogram. Local residents fear that this could expose Parki beach, the Water Development Board embankment and the Karnaphuli Tunnel service area, built at a cost of Tk 503 crore, to erosion risk. The upazila administration said there is no approval for extracting sand from the river next to the beach. On a Monday visit the reporter saw two bulkheads and a dredger at sea near the tunnel service area, and two booster machines on the shore. Sand was being piped to fill land for a power plant under construction. Residents said extraction had continued for the past 12 days. Sand was taken through a pipeline laid through the casuarina grove, stored in bulkheads and sent through a pipeline of about one kilometre. The report said Dhaka-based contractor Premier Company is doing the filling with the help of political leaders of Barashat union, supervised by supervisor Md. Saiful Islam and 10 to 15 workers. The Forest Department planted casuarina on about 80 hectares in and around Parki in 1993-94 and 2002. Residents Habib, Hasan and Azgar alleged that Premier does the extraction but is absent from the project signboard, and claimed there is uncertainty about port authority approval. Saiful Islam said Premier was only engaged for filling and that the project contractor hired the bulkhead, dredger and two booster machines; he said he did not know the sand source or whether permission exists. Premier engineer Mohammad Ismail said they extract from a specified place on the Karnaphuli with Chattogram Port Authority permission and claimed extraction is not possible with a bulkhead and dredger at sea. Anwara Assistant Commissioner (Land) Md. Abu Zafar Majumder said there is no approval and that action will be taken after finding who is extracting. Representatives of the entities on the signboard could not be reached.

records.titleEn: ‘If stone extraction resumes, Sylhet’s environment will be under threat’
records.dateEvidence: Report of a BELA exchange meeting with quotes from BELA coordinator Advocate Shah Saheda and participants; minister's announcement reported second-hand
records.location: Sylhet division (Sylhet district; Sylhet-4 constituency covering Goainghat, Jaintapur and Companiganj)
rivers: Quarry areas of Sylhet with rivers, hills and tilas mentioned generally
records.summary: Environmental activists voiced concern that reopening Sylhet's closed stone quarries would again threaten the environment and ecosystem. They said seven of the district's eight stone quarries lie in tourism-rich areas, so extraction could harm rivers, hills, tilas and biodiversity. A meeting heard that Labour Minister and Sylhet-4 (Goainghat-Jaintapur-Companiganj) MP Ariful Haque Chowdhury had announced the quarries would soon be opened by 'traditional methods'. At a Tuesday (22 September) exchange meeting organised by the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA) on the status of its cases in Sylhet division, the 32 writs BELA has filed on Sylhet's environmental issues were reviewed. BELA Sylhet divisional coordinator Advocate Shah Saheda said that although quarries are closed on paper under court orders, extraction has not stopped in Sylhet, and court-ordered bans on hill (tila) cutting have not fully stopped it. She said authorities mostly do not follow court directions, and called the minister's announcement contempt of court given the court ban on stone extraction. Participants said quarries are ecologically linked to rivers, hills, tilas, forests and tourism, and long-term environmental impact should be considered before reopening. BELA's Nirupam Dey moderated; network members from four districts of Sylhet division took part.
records.limitations: Claims by environmental activists; minister's announcement reported indirectly, not verified; no site-level extraction data Collected 2026-11-18 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 2685 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.dateEvidence: Source page: September 8th, 2026
records.location: Northern Province, Rulindo District, Rusine River watershed (Rutongo Mining Concession)
records.summary: This preprint studies artisanal alluvial tin and aggregate (sand, gravel, stone) mining in the Rusine River watershed in Rulindo District. records.dateEvidence: Peer-unreviewed preprint based on 13 in-depth interviews with workers, plus cited literature and BBS data
records.location: Tetulia Union, Panchagarh district (northernmost district of Bangladesh)
records.summary: This research article, posted online on 12 August 2026, studies riverine stone quarry workers along the Mahananda River in Tetulia Union, Panchagarh district. It uses testimonio-style in-depth interviews with 13 male workers (fieldwork March 2025) and inductive thematic analysis. Participants had worked in the sector for at least one year; the participant table lists ages from 20 to 56 and 6 to 40 years of work experience. The authors report that irregular work, dependence on stone traders, declining earnings, untreated injuries and restrictions in a militarised border zone combine to produce "organised precarity". Workers described themselves as living in a "sandwich graveyard" between Border Guard Bangladesh and India's Border Security Force. Background: the paper cites the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (2023) saying the informal sector employs more than 85% of the national workforce. It cites local estimates (Alam & Pradhan, 2022) that nearly 40,000 people are directly involved in stone quarrying in the region. It says there is no official government registry of stone quarry workers. The supplied text is truncated, so the full findings are not included.
records.limitations: Preprint not yet peer reviewed; small purposive/snowball sample of 13 men; extract is truncated; the 40,000 figure is a local estimate cited from another source Collected 2026-11-16 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 62540 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.dateEvidence: Quotes from the tourism magistrate, an NCP organiser and a BAPA member; witnesses and local sources; seizure of equipment at the site
records.location: Kolatoli beach, south part near Bhangar Mor, Cox's Bazar Sadar, Cox's Bazar
records.summary: Dhaka Post reported that a syndicate was secretly extracting sand from Cox's Bazar sea beach using an illegally laid pipeline and a special machine. A district administration tourism branch team reached the site around 1 am on 8 August (the night of Friday 7 August), at the southern part of the Kolatoli beach near Bhangar Mor. No one involved was found, but a large quantity of geo bags, a sand-extraction machine, large pipes and other evidence were located. Tourism magistrate (assistant commissioner) Mohammad Mahmudur Rahman Sayem told Dhaka Post the operation was based on information from local youths. He said sand was being taken through a water pipeline set up in a building near the dunes, where many geo bags were found. He said three beach workers were deployed at the spot and the evidence was being seized, with further action under way. Witnesses and local sources said the building houses the 'Blue Economy Service and Consultation Centre' run by the NGO Integrated Development Foundation (IDF); no one from the institution could be reached for comment immediately. NCP Cox's Bazar Sadar upazila organising secretary Arian Farabi said he saw sand being illegally extracted with a dredger while walking on the beach at night, collected evidence and video, and informed the tourism magistrate and law enforcement; the people involved had fled by the time officials arrived. He called for exposing any influential backing. BAPA central committee member Karim Ullah Kalim demanded an immediate end to illegal extraction and permanent protection of the beach and dunes. The report gives no volume or quantity of sand extracted.
records.limitations: Allegations by witnesses and activists; IDF had no comment available; no sand quantity or arrests reported Collected 2026-11-11 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 2949 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.title: The plunder that never stopped: Illegal stone, sand extraction persist in Bangladesh’s Sylhet
records.titleEn: The plunder that never stopped: Illegal stone, sand extraction persist in Bangladesh’s Sylhet
records.publisher: The Daily Star via Asia News Network
records.dateEvidence: Reporters' site visits, resident, official, activist and minister quotations, and cited case and ministry actions
records.location: Bichhanakandi and Jaflong (Gowainghat); Sada Pathor, Shah Arefin Tila, Utmachhara, Railway Bunker (Companiganj); Lobhachhara (Kanaighat); Sreepur, Rangpani, Borogang (Jaintiapur); Sylhet district
records.summary: Correspondents who visited sites in Sylhet district reported organised groups extracting stone and sand unchecked, at night and dawn, including at Bichhanakandi on the Piyain river. Named areas are Bichhanakandi and Jaflong in Gowainghat; Sada Pathor, Shah Arefin Tila, Utmachhara and Railway Bunker in Companiganj; Lobhachhara in Kanaighat; and Sreepur, Rangpani and Borogang in Jaintiapur. Eight BOMD-gazetted quarries were leased for manual extraction for more than two decades until 2020. Jaflong’s 14.93-square-kilometre area was declared an Ecologically Critical Area in 2015, and a court banned mechanical extraction at all eight quarries in 2014. The paper says machines still dug deep pits and extraction spread beyond quarry boundaries. After the government fell on August 5, 2024, looting spread; the administration estimated stones worth Tk 200 crore were taken from Jaflong alone within days since August 2024, and the 15-acre Bholaganj Sada Pathor tourist site was stripped bare within a year. Dhora’s Abdul Karim Kim said the plundering far exceeds the past 15 years’ looting. The DoE filed a case against 31 people, including four local BNP leaders, on March 25, 2025. On April 27, 2025 the environment ministry banned leasing of all 17 stone quarries nationwide, including the eight in Sylhet. BOMD filed a case against unnamed people on August 15, 2025; Rab arrested upazila BNP president Sahab Uddin the following month; the ACC began a probe in August 2025, and its preliminary report found involvement of officials, law enforcers and political leaders, with the final report not yet submitted. Syndicates, allegedly backed by local BNP leaders, continued extraction. Residents said sand removal around Jaflong Bridge (Gowainghat) and Dhalai Bridge (Companiganj) pillars raised collapse fears, and looters were digging beneath the 500-year-old Jaflong Palace. Residents said extraction alters river flow and may worsen erosion. Officials gave differing accounts: the DoE’s Abul Kalam Azad said no stones are extracted in Jaflong’s ECA; BOMD’s Mohammad Rabiul Faysal said seized material is sold by tender and mobile courts are held twice a month; acting DC Pinki Saha said drives continue. On May 7, 2026 the home minister announced a committee on limited extraction in Sylhet and Sunamganj, and on June 24 minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said quarries would reopen for manual extraction; activists and lawyers opposed this, citing High Court orders.

records.title: অবৈধ বালু উত্তোলনে রাজস্ব হারাচ্ছে সরকার
records.titleEn: Government losing revenue due to illegal sand extraction
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's account, local residents' statements, quotes from the Kamalganj UNO and a BELA coordinator, and a described High Court order
records.location: Kamalganj upazila, Moulvibazar district
rivers: Deochhara, Sunchhara, Joplachhara, Lawachhara and other hill streams (chhara) in Kamalganj and Moulvibazar district
records.summary: The report says silica sand is being extracted freely, day and night, from around a hundred or more hill streams (chhara) in Moulvibazar district, including in Kamalganj upazila. Named streams are Deochhara, Sunchhara, Joplachhara and Lawachhara. It says an influential group is destroying the environment without effective administrative action, so streams, mounds (tila) and farmland are being damaged and the government is losing a large amount of revenue (no amount is given). It states the district has 33 silica sand quarries approved by the Bureau of Mineral Development. According to the report, on 18 June 2013 a notification declared 51 hill streams in the district silica-sand-bearing areas (the text attributes this to the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association, BELA), and 19 of them were leased for non-mechanised extraction. It says uncontrolled and illegal extraction by lessees caused severe environmental damage. BELA filed a public-interest writ petition on 8 March 2016, and on 21 March a High Court Division bench barred further leasing of the 19 sand mahals without an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and Environmental Clearance Certificate (ECC). The report says the order is being ignored. Locals said a politically influential local group is involved in the sand trade; it uses labourers, carries sand by truck, pickup, trolley and pushcart, and leaves when the administration approaches. Kamalganj Upazila Executive Officer Md. Asaduzzaman said he inspected Deochhara after an application to the deputy commissioner and sent the assistant commissioner (land) on Wednesday but found no one; he said drives against extraction from other streams continue. BELA Sylhet divisional coordinator Adv. Shah Saheda Akhter said extraction without a lease is illegal, the administration must stop it, and those enabling it are defying the High Court. The report warns that without strict action the streams and mounds could vanish from the district map in 10 years.
records.limitations: Residents' allegations about an influential group; no revenue figure given; the text mixes up BELA with the notification issuer; date not shown in the article text Collected 2026-11-18 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 2358 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.summary: Analyzing DSAS shoreline transects from 2009 to 2023 along the Vinh Long coast between the Co Chien and Hau mouths, this study links delta coastal retreat to sediment starvation and coastal structures. Reduced fluvial sand and mud delivery leaves the mangrove fringe unable to keep pace with wave energy.

records.title: Teesta riverbanks can be saved through embankments, dredging: Minister Anee
records.titleEn: Teesta riverbanks can be saved through embankments, dredging: Minister Anee
records.dateEvidence: Minister's statements at an exchange meeting after a site inspection, as reported by the bdnews24.com Lalmonirhat correspondent
records.location: Teesta Barrage, Hatibandha Upazila, Lalmonirhat
records.summary: Water Resources Minister Shahid Uddin Chowdhury Anee said on Friday, after inspecting the Teesta Barrage in Hatibandha Upazila, Lalmonirhat, that well-planned embankments and dredging could permanently protect people living along the Teesta from river erosion and flooding. He said a technical team and experts had gathered at the prime minister's direction to work out how to tackle the problem. He said India opening the gates of the Gajoldoba Barrage creates a powerful rush of water that makes the Teesta banks give way, and that sustainable embankments and dredging would be fast-tracked. Describing the Teesta Master Plan as essential for the whole country, he said completing the visible work may take two to four years, or even six to seven years, and that the suffering of five districts would then turn into productivity. He said several more meetings would be held before a special seminar at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology, after which the project would go to the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council for final approval, modelled on the Padma Barrage project. The report gives no dredging volumes, costs or specific dredging sites.

records.dateEvidence: News report citing unnamed sources, an injured local resident, local residents' allegations and the OC of Ramgarh police station
records.location: Purba Balipara area, Ramgarh union, Ramgarh upazila, Khagrachhari
records.summary: A report dated 12 May 2026 says a mobile court operation against illegal sand extraction in the Purba Balipara area of Ramgarh union, Ramgarh upazila, Khagrachhari, led to a clash with local people. The report names no river. At least 10 people on both sides, including the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO), were injured. The incident happened between about 3pm and 4pm on Tuesday 12 May. Acting on a tip-off, UNO Kazi Shamim ran the mobile court, with law enforcement members led by Ramgarh police OC Mohammad Nazir Alam present. The administration destroyed six to seven selo machines and sand-transport pipes used in the extraction. Local residents alleged that selo machines and pipes that some farmers used to irrigate their land were also smashed. Locals then chased the officials and clashed with them. Six members of the operation team, including the UNO, were injured by bricks and stones thrown by the crowd. To control the situation and protect the mobile court members, Ansar members fired five to six rounds of rubber bullets from a shotgun; four locals were injured in the clash at that time. The injured were taken to Ramgarh Upazila Health Complex and received primary treatment; sources said none was in critical condition. Injured local Abul Hashem said Ansar members shot at them when they went to protest over the damaged irrigation equipment, and that they were hurt by those shots. The UNO told journalists nothing. The OC said the area was normal, no complaint had been filed at the police station so far, and legal action would follow an investigation once a complaint is lodged.

records.title: ‘ভাগেযোগে’ পাথর লুট, সুউচ্চ-সবুজ শাহ আরেফিন টিলা এখন ‘সাগর’
records.titleEn: Stone looted through 'sharing arrangements'; the tall, green Shah Arefin Tila is now a 'sea'
records.dateEvidence: Reporter site visit; interviews with residents, a lawyer, environmentalists and officials (DC, OC, SP, MP); BELA data; ACC case details; police and administration records cited
records.location: Shah Arefin Tila (Chikadohor mouza), Companiganj upazila, Sylhet; Bholaganj area
records.summary: bdnews24 reported on 6 May 2026 (updated 26 August 2026) that Shah Arefin Tila, in Chikadohor mouza, Companiganj upazila, Sylhet, has been ravaged by stone extraction over nearly two decades. The report names no river. It says the hill now has at least 100 holes, 20 to 300 feet deep; lawyer Farhad Khandaker put the depth at 20 to 200 feet. The paper said political leaders and corrupt administration and law-enforcement officials are alleged to have installed illegal 'bomb machines' on a sharing ('bhageyoge') basis. It also said at least 200 such machines are in the area, which a local youth repeated. The article notes the High Court banned these machines about two decades ago. Locals said looting surged after the political change of 5 August 2024 and again after the 13th parliamentary election, and that about 90 percent of the stone is gone. The hill sits on 137.50 acres of government khas land, with stone in about 350 more acres around it; 10 acres were waqf land for the shrine. The quarry was last leased for one year in April 2005. A 2009 Department of Environment report (published 11 November) called the hill a 'skeleton'. Stone is piled in villages and fields at Noagaon, Babulnagar, Jaliarpar, Shah Arefin Bazar and Chikadohor. Bholaganj traders said Shah Arefin stone sells to crusher owners at Tk 90-92 per cubic foot; crushers sell 'single' stone at Tk 130-135, half-inch at Tk 70 and 3x4 at Tk 160-162 per cubic foot. Locals alleged that at least 100 trolleys and tractors carry stone to Bholaganj daily, each making 2-3 trips of at least 50 cubic feet, and that each trip pays Tk 200 to patrolling police. They also alleged an 'OC line' of at least 100 tractors making two trips each, last run on 17 March from 3am to 6am. Companiganj OC Md Shafiqul Islam Khan called the allegations false; Sylhet SP Chowdhury Md Jaber Sadek said he knew nothing of it and that action would follow any complaint. DC Md Sarwar Alam said the hill is gone and 'made into a sea'. BELA said 38 workers died in hole collapses between 14 February 2005 and 14 December 2021, with several hundred more injured. Six workers died on 23 January 2017, and in 2017 task force drives (43 operations) destroyed 168 bomb machines. A district committee report implicated 47 people, and a 2018 district administration report identified 87 'stone-eaters'. The ACC case, filed in October 2021 against Mohammad Ali (40) of Bashir Company, alleges 62,88,750 cubic feet of stone was taken from 137.5 acres, yielding Tk 252 crore 55 lakh 90 thousand in illegal assets. Elsewhere the article gives the value as Tk 252 crore 75 lakh. The lease covered 61 acres with 13 conditions, and the case is ongoing. On 9 April authorities seized 96,800 cubic feet of stone. On 20 March a joint drive seized 39 stone-laden tractors. A case over the attack on police during that drive was filed against 14 named people and 8-10 unnamed.
records.limitations: Many claims are allegations by locals; police and named individuals denied involvement; article shows both Published and Updated dates; headline and body give slightly different ACC amounts (Tk 252.75 crore vs Tk 252.55 crore). Fresh March 24 observations and quantities distinguish it from existing March 20 seizure coverage; all rates, prices, allegations and competing officials' counts retained separately.
records.location: Sylhet
records.summary: Prothom Alo's 6 April 2026 investigation reports fresh 24 March observations of stone extraction at Shah Arefin Tila, Companiganj, Sylhet, beyond the already reported 20 March seizure. The government hill site covers 137.50 acres, with stones in about 350 adjoining acres; two former hillocks have been depleted over roughly 25 years since around 2000, with further looting after 5 August 2024. Reporters described pits 20–300 feet deep, while the DC separately described 100–150-foot pits. Crushers near Bholaganj, Guchhagram, Parua and Dakghar lie at least 4km away; reporters saw 27 sand-covered stone trolleys in three hours on 24 March through nearby village roads. Traders quoted raw stone at Tk90–92 per 'foot'; crusher prices were Tk130–135 for single stone, Tk70 for half-inch stone and Tk160–162 for 3-by-4 stone per 'foot'. The article does not explicitly define that trading unit as cubic feet. Local sources alleged about 100 trolleys daily, each making 2–3 trips with at least 50 'feet' per load, and Tk200 paid to patrolling police per trip. They also alleged a weekly night route involving at least 100 tractors averaging two trips; a resident identified 17 March, 3–6am, as the latest such run. These are attributed estimates and allegations, not audited flows or proven bribery. The report cites 39 tractors seized on 20 March and a subsequent case naming 14 people plus 8–10 unidentified accused; the SP separately referred to 40 tractors seized recently, without establishing that these were an additional batch. Some accused denied involvement, including one saying he had not been involved for four months; the OC denied police facilitation, while the SP invited specific complaints. Officials said enforcement continued and a police outpost was proposed. Reports of limited extraction at Kalairag, Dayarbazar, the Bholaganj bunker, Rangpani–Sripur and Lovachhara remain attributed; Sada Pathor, Utmachhara and Bichhanakandi were described as stopped.
records.limitations: Attributed police/political allegations and denials; source's feet trading units not silently converted; 39 and 40 tractor statements not added together.

records.title: Sand mining and Kenya’s building boom: Better rules are needed, but not from the top down
records.titleEn: Sand mining and Kenya's building boom: Better rules are needed, but not from the top down
records.publisher: Down To Earth (republished from The Conversation)
records.dateEvidence: Source page: Published on : 18 Feb 2026, 5:04 am
records.location: National scope; study sites in Homa Bay, Nakuru (Kedong), Kajiado, Taita Taveta, Makueni, Kwale and Kilifi
records.summary: Researchers Kennedy Mkutu and Jan Bachmann summarise a study of sand commodity chains at sites in seven Kenyan counties, including Homa Bay near Lake Victoria and Nakuru. They say national regulation is rarely enforced and informal rules among loaders, cooperatives and landowners govern extraction. In Kajiado, a driver pays loaders around $10 each and the landowner $40-$50. They report drivers pay around $90 for a 12-ton truck that sells in Nairobi for up to $400, and police request $4-8 per truck. At Kedong in Nakuru, residents destroyed landowners' excavators. They argue for harmonising informal rules with formal ones, citing Makueni.
records.limitations: Commentary summarising the authors' own research; the original is on The Conversation (not fetched). Prices are approximate US-dollar figures. records.titleEn: Impact of Selected Anthropogenic Disturbances on the Variability of Riparian Vegetation in the River Kathita Basin, Tharaka Nithi County, Kenya
records.publisher: East African Journal of Environment and Natural Resources (EANSO)
records.authors: Denis Kibaara Mugambi; Rithaa Jafford Njeru; Agatha Nthenge
records.dateEvidence: Source page: 23 September, 2025
records.location: Tharaka Nithi County, River Kathita basin
records.summary: This open-access Chuka University study compares riparian vegetation at sand harvesting, charcoal burning and livestock drinking sites with undisturbed control sites, randomly sampled along a 15KM transect, in the River Kathita basin, Tharaka-Nithi County. Disturbed sites showed lower species diversity than undisturbed sites. The correlation with tree diversity was significant for livestock grazing (p=0.01) and marginally insignificant for sand harvesting and charcoal burning (p=0.06). Abandoned sand harvesting sites had high seedling and sapling diversity, suggesting recovery if protected. The authors recommend that local and national stakeholders regulate sand harvesting in riparian areas.
records.limitations: Ecological vegetation study; sand harvesting is one of three disturbances examined, and its statistical association was not significant at p<0.05. No extraction volumes.

records.title: How Bangladesh’s sole granite mining company is finally moving towards profitability
records.titleEn: How Bangladesh’s sole granite mining company is finally moving towards profitability
records.dateEvidence: Interview statements by Maddhapara Deputy General Manager Syed Rofizul Islam, company data cited as 'available data', traders' price comments, and reference to a previous TBS report.
records.location: Maddhapara mine, Parbatipur upazila, Dinajpur
records.summary: TBS reported that Maddhapara Granite Mining Company, a Petrobangla-operated underground mine in Parbatipur upazila, Dinajpur district, has set a production record. Company officials said its granite was sidelined in favour of imported Indian stone that they called inferior, and TBS reported the mine lost nearly Tk30 crore in 2024. Deputy General Manager Syed Rofizul Islam said the monthly target is 124,000 tonnes and that over the past eight months extraction exceeded the target by nearly 400,000 tonnes. He said annual national stone demand is 21.6 million tonnes, mostly imported from India, Bhutan and Dubai, with a negligible local supply from the Mahananda River in Panchagarh and the Bholaganj area of Sylhet. He said Bangladesh Railway and the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) had stopped buying under pressure from the previous government but are now reconnecting, and that about Tk400 crore worth of stone is stocked; he said he is confident the company will return to profit. The stockpile exceeds 1.2 million tonnes, including about 750,000 tonnes of the railway type; the railway has signed for 100,000 tonnes and has collected 60,000. A previous TBS report said Tk30 crore was borrowed in August last year to settle dues with the contractor. Daily extraction is about 5,500 tonnes (over 1.5 million tonnes a year) against annual sales of about 900,000 tonnes. By size: 18% 5–20 mm, 5% 20–40 mm, 34% 40–60 mm (blast), 11% 60–80 mm, 17% boulder and 15% dust (0–5 mm); blast and boulder stone make up 51% of output. Most construction needs 8–12 mm stone, which the mine does not produce, so many users take 5–20 mm, for which demand exceeds the mine's capacity. Stock as of 31 May 2025 included 780,000 tonnes of blast stone suitable for railway use and 452,000 tonnes of boulders used in river training projects. Prices per tonne: 0–5 mm Tk1,150; 5–20 mm Tk3,250; 20–40 mm Tk3,600; 40–60 mm Tk3,650; 60–80 mm Tk2,600; boulder Tk3,200; fine dust Tk740. Quarry officials and traders said the 2006 marketing guideline (revised 2017), which requires advance booking, cash payment at banks and self-arranged transport, discourages individual buyers. Traders said imported Indian 5–20 mm stone costs Tk120–130 per cubic foot against Tk140 for Maddhapara stone. The 65-km dedicated rail line became defunct within six months of operation and 8.8 km of track was stolen in early 2023. Trucking costs Tk1,200–1,300 per tonne from Maddhapara to Dhaka and Tk2,100–2,200 to Chattogram; Rofizul Islam said that if the railway were restored, costs could fall to Tk400–500 per tonne to Dhaka and Tk900–1,000 to Chattogram.
records.limitations: Company official's account and projections (e.g. profitability hopes, stock value); figures not independently verified; the feature is about a managed mine and its commercial performance rather than illegal extraction. records.titleEn: Why is the 'White Stone' site environmentally important, and what are the harmful impacts?
records.dateEvidence: BBC report with quotes from environmentalists, the Sylhet deputy commissioner, a local teacher and a local journalist; local residents' accounts; media videos
records.location: Bholaganj Zero Point, Companiganj upazila, Sylhet
rivers: Dhalai river (Dhalai nad) source area, Bholaganj Zero Point
records.summary: A BBC report published on 12 August 2025 says stone looting has continued without pause at the Bholaganj Shada Pathor (White Stone) tourist spot at Bholaganj Zero Point, at the source of the Dhalai river (nad) in Companiganj upazila, Sylhet, since 5 August of the previous year. Companiganj is a border upazila 35 km from Sylhet city. Sand is also being taken along with the stone. The report says that before 5 August the area was covered in white stones, but it is now a bare sandbar. An unattributed account ('their words'; the source does not say who) puts the loss at 15 million cubic feet (1 crore 50 lakh cubic feet) of stone looted in one year, with an estimated market value of more than Tk 200 crore (2,000 million). Four BGB camps and posts surround the tourist site. The site, formed over about five acres by stones washed down by hill torrents, became a popular tourist spot; a local teacher said this happened from 2012, after road improvements cut the trip from Sylhet city to about 40 minutes. Environmentalist Kasmir Reza, general secretary of Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon's Sylhet district unit, alleged that local influential people are removing stone illegally and that no effective administrative drive is visible. He said a court injunction bars removing stone from Bholaganj, the site has not been leased, and no stone was extracted there in the past four years. Sylhet Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Sher Mahbub Murad said action is ongoing, with nearly daily drives, mobile courts, task force operations and regular cases. He said a meeting had been called for the next day to understand why looting continues. Locals said only stones near a BGB camp, within 100 metres of the site, now remain. On Monday, the administration and law enforcers ran a drive and disabled the boats used to carry stone away. Local journalist Mahbubur Rahman Ripon said nobody came to loot on Tuesday and attributed the looting to administrative inaction or fear. Media videos showed stone being carried off by boat and dug from pits earlier that week. Environmentalist and architect Iqbal Habib said the stones control water flow and add oxygen, and that removing them could increase flooding on both sides, cause erosion and pollute the water, which supplies drinking water to parts of the area.

BELA Sylhet divisional coordinator Shah Shaheda Akhter said stones worth about Tk 2000 crore were illegally extracted from Sylhet quarries in the last 10 months. Local sources say much of the stone goes to Meghalaya, India, often illegally. Sylhet UNO Md. Touhidul Islam said extraction without a valid lease has been stopped on ministry orders, but full prevention is difficult because of local influential people. Adviser Syeda Rizwana Hasan said no new quarry will open in sensitive areas like Jaflong.

records.title: অভিযানেও থামছে না ফসলি জমির মাটি কাটা
records.titleEn: Even operations fail to stop cutting of soil from farmland
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's account citing a mobile court operation, the UNO's statement, upazila agriculture office sources and unnamed multiple sources
records.location: Satkania upazila, Chattogram (Chhankhola in Aochia union; Temuhani in Keochia union; also Aochia and Kanchana unions; North Dhemsha and Temuhani mouzas)
rivers: Agricultural land and hillside areas in Satkania
records.summary: Shomoyer Alo reported that topsoil cutting on farmland continues in Satkania upazila, Chattogram, despite administrative operations. Soil traders were said to be cutting fertile topsoil with excavators in various areas, and many farmers were selling their soil for short-term financial gain; the local agriculture department feared a sharp fall in crop production. On the night of Friday 10 January, from midnight to 4 am, a mobile court ran an operation in Chhankhola (Aochia union) and Temuhani (Keochia union) on a tip-off. Those involved fled on seeing the magistrate and left their excavators; two excavators were seized. Executive magistrate and Satkania UNO Milton Biswas ordered regular cases to be filed at the police station against those involved. An earlier mobile court on the night of 6 January in Aochia and Kanchana unions also saw offenders flee, and one excavator was seized. Despite this, allegations say topsoil is still cut and sold to brick kilns, with cutting starting at night. Multiple sources said soil traders post lookouts on roads to the upazila parishad, land office and police station to give advance warning of raids. The report says the most brick kilns are in North Dhemsha, South Dhemsha, Temuhani, Rasulabad and South Chhadaha, with 10-12 kilns beside the hills at Aochia Churamoni and Chhankhola near the Banshkhali border. It also alleged that during the Awami era party people cut soil from hundreds of hectares of farmland in North Dhemsha and Temuhani mouzas beside the under-construction rail line on the Chattogram-Cox's Bazar highway, turning it into a large lake. Upazila agriculture office sources said arable land is shrinking and production may fall sharply. UNO Milton Biswas said the operations continue and strict steps are being taken to stop it permanently.
records.limitations: Several claims are allegations from unnamed sources, including the sale to brick kilns, lookouts and the past lake formation attributed to party people Collected 2026-11-11 by GitHub Actions (firecrawl read, 5678 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.titleEn: Intensified susceptibility to riverbed incisions under sand mining impacts in the Vietnamese mekong delta: A long-term spatiotemporal analysis
records.authors: Menna Farag Ahmed, Doan Van Binh, Sameh A. Kantoush, Edward Park, Nguyen Luyen Phuong Doan, Anh Tuan Luc, Nguyen Dinh Vuong, Thi Huong Vu, Binh Quang Nguyen, Anh Ngoc Trieu, Xuan Tung Nguyen and Tetsuya Sumi

records.title: Dammed in the Mekong: Averting an Environmental Catastrophe
records.titleEn: Dammed in the Mekong: Averting an Environmental Catastrophe
records.dateEvidence: Report header and dateline: Report 343 / Asia-Pacific, 07 October 2024
records.location: Mekong basin (excluding Myanmar in field interviews)
records.summary: Crisis Group Asia Report No. 343 examines the cumulative governance, ecological and human-security risks of hydropower (661 operational dams) and sand mining across the Mekong basin. Its sand-mining analysis cites delta extraction averaging 43 million m³/year (2015–2020)—14 to 17 times natural replenishment—and 2007–2016 Cambodia-to-Singapore trade discrepancies (nearly 3 million tonnes reported exported versus >80 million tonnes reported imported), alongside 585 delta erosion hotspots spanning >740 km. It recommends integrating sand-mining monitoring into the MRC’s Core Monitoring Function and National Mekong Committees.
records.limitations: Policy synthesis report based on literature review and 2022–2024 interviews; quantitative sand-mining and erosion figures are cited from published studies and Vietnamese authorities rather than new field measurements, and Myanmar was excluded from fieldwork.

records.dateEvidence: Source page: August 19th, 2024
records.location: Homa Bay County, Kobala village / Kobala sub-location (Lake Victoria shore)
records.summary: Taifa Leo reports that in Kobala village, Homa Bay County, sand digging has left deep pits, hanging houses and exposed graves, with coffin parts and human bones surfacing. Resident Willis Omullo said it began 15 years ago when sand extraction intensified, that at least a quarter of the village has been dug up, and that eight houses once stood on land now swamped. He said some digging takes place below the lake water level, and that families themselves dig their own land. Former digger Karen Juma Odera said it took her four days to fill a lorry, for which she was paid Sh1,000.
records.limitations: Swahili feature based on residents' testimony; no official comment. The lede refers to gravel diggers (wachimbaji changarawe) while the body describes sand digging; extraction is on family land along the lakeshore. English translation of the headline awaits Swahili review.

records.title: The plunder of Piyain: sand-looting frenzy devastates river ecosystem, communities
records.titleEn: The plunder of Piyain: sand-looting frenzy devastates river ecosystem, communities
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's site visit on a Friday, villager and local representative interviews, and responses from officials, party leaders, police and environmental groups
records.location: West Jaflong union, Gowainghat Upazila, Sylhet
rivers: Piyain River (Hadarpar Bazar, Munaikandi, Noagram, Bugalkandi
records.summary: bdnews24.com reported on 19 June 2024 that villagers in at least six villages of West Jaflong union, Gowainghat Upazila, Sylhet, alleged that dredger-based sand mining on the Piyain River, with no lease or designated sand reserve, was being facilitated by ruling Awami League activists 'managing' the local administration. Villagers said homes, land, madrasas, schools and graveyards were eroding; graveyards at Munaikandi and Noagram were crumbling into the river. Ward 1 Awami League president Islam Uddin said more than a hundred locally made dredgers ('bomb machines') operated from 8pm to 9am. The reporter saw at least 15 dredger boats moored at Hadarpar Bazar around 9:30am and dredgers on four large boats near Munaikandi madrasa around 11:30am; locals said 10 to 15 dredgers filled boats by day. Haji Mohammed Ali, 70, said 50 to 60 boats worked all night; Ashfor Mia said about 5,000 houses in four wards on both sides of the river were at risk; ward member Abul Kadir said hundreds of excavators worked from evening to 6am; Abul Kalam said 400-500 boats leave every day. The article says the Piyain flows about 150 km as a border river from Assam, then about 80 km in Sylhet and Sunamganj. A local businessman alleged extortion from sand boats and named district council members; Subas Das denied involvement. Locals alleged two police officers and a constable took money; the police station chief denied police involvement. Union Awami League president Shafiq Ahmed denied allegations as politically motivated. A villager's relative, Bushra Begum, said her brother was attacked with a machete after opposing dredging. UNO Md Tauhidul Islam said law enforcers would act against mining outside designated plots; additional divisional commissioner Md Jasim Uddin said action would follow for unleased extraction; Department of Environment's AKM Rafiqul Islam said it would investigate. Environmentalists at a 12 June meeting said illegal mining continues and the administration has failed. The Jadukata River in Tahirpur, Sunamganj, is cited as a comparison.
records.limitations: Largely allegations by residents and local figures, denied by those named; the page shows an Updated date of 21 Aug 2026 in addition to the published date Collected 2026-11-19 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 14017 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.location: Abu Danga river area, Jiyanpur union, Daulatpur upazila, Manikganj
rivers: Jamuna connecting canal (Jamuna char and other waterways also mentioned)
records.summary: Protidiner Sangbad reported on 19 March 2024 that illegal dredger-based sand extraction continues in Daulatpur upazila, Manikganj. Influential people were said to be extracting sand from rivers, canals, wetlands, the Jamuna char and ponds across the upazila. On a site visit the previous day (Tuesday), the reporter saw 2 dredgers running day and night in the Abu Danga river in Jiyanpur union, and 2 more dredgers cutting sand in a canal connected to the Jamuna. The paper reported that soil had collapsed on both sides of the canal, leaving huge holes. Local residents feared riverbanks and farmland would be badly damaged. One person who asked not to be named said about 3-4 dredgers were operating around Abu Danga and Bishnupur, and that nobody speaks up because the owners are influential. The person also said that when the administration acts, the operators resume after a few days. Dredger owner Rezaul was quoted as saying the administration's drives would continue, but that he runs his dredger on his own power. Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Ashikur Rahman Chowdhury said he conducted a drive there some days earlier and would conduct another.
records.limitations: Anonymous source and residents' allegations; influence claims unverified; exact location of the Jamuna-connected canal not specified Collected 2026-11-11 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 2071 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.titleEn: Illegal sand extraction continues without permission | SATV
records.dateEvidence: TV channel's online report quoting an environmental activist, an engineer and the Feni Deputy Commissioner; no figures on volumes or fines
records.location: Feni district (Sonapur government Asrayan project area mentioned)
rivers: Sand mahals and char areas in Feni
topics: Crop land and housing project erosion
records.summary: SATV online reported (Updated 3 March 2024) that sand is being extracted illegally without approval in Feni district; the report names no river, upazila or union. It said crop land, a housing project and an agriculture department scheme project are being eroded, the government is losing revenue, and the environment is being harmed. Of Feni's eight legal sand mahals, three have reportedly not been leased for many years. The report said influential people are illegally seizing sand, harming river navigability, environment and biodiversity, and that extraction continues even after the lease terms of the legal mahals expired. Local residents are at risk of losing their homes. The report said that, after leases were taken at nominal prices, crop land on emerged chars outside the lease areas is being cut by dredger machines day and night. It said the Sonapur government Asrayan (shelter) project is disappearing because of the illegal extraction. An environmental activist said biodiversity is being damaged. The report said the administration sometimes conducts drives but has not stopped the influential. Engineer Rashed Shahriar said cases are filed constantly and government development projects will be destroyed if these activities do not stop. The Feni Deputy Commissioner said strict instructions have been given to all UNOs and cases will be filed against illegal extractors if needed. The report says Feni has about 15 sand mahals, large and small, of which only 8 are leased. It gives no volumes or fines.

records.title: চেল্লাখালী নদীতে চলছে অবৈধ বালু উত্তোলন
records.titleEn: Illegal sand extraction is going on in the Chellakhali river
records.dateEvidence: Reporter site visit; phone calls with Rasul Mahmud and lease-holder Zobayer Hossain Sohel; statements from a union leader and the upazila executive officer; resident allegations
records.location: Burunga village near Baromari bazar, Nalitabari upazila, Sherpur district
rivers: Chellakhali river (Burunga bridge on the border road)
records.summary: Desh TV reported on 3 March 2024 that sand is being extracted illegally from the hilly Chellakhali river in the Garo hills border area of Nalitabari upazila, Sherpur district. The report says the Burunga bridge on the border road is under threat, along with crop fields and homes. According to the report, some unscrupulous lease-holders and local illegal sand traders use local influence to extract sand around the bridge and from riverside farmland. Residents alleged that the extractors, being influential, extract at will with many shallow machines (Selo machines), openly in daylight. The report says deep pits are forming and farmland is collapsing, and the pillar piling of the bridge has been exposed as the soil beneath it washed away. Residents said the government-granted balumahal lease is two kilometres from the bridge. The report says a local influential trader, Rasul Mahmud, is illegally extracting sand from government khas land in Burunga village beside Baromari bazar, putting an electricity pole, an irrigation drain, a mosque and several houses at risk. Many victims said that people who object face threats, beatings and lawsuits. About 200 or more workers from Burunga, Andharupara and Khalchanda villages are involved in extraction and transport; Poragaon Workers' Union general secretary Badsha Miah said they want sand extracted legally. Rasul Mahmud told the reporter by phone that he is extracting legally. The main lease-holder, former Chhatra League leader Zobayer Hossain Sohel, gave no satisfactory answer. Nalitabari Upazila Executive Officer Risil said they often run drives to stop illegal extraction and will act if needed on receiving a written complaint when it restarts. Victims said written complaints to the upazila administration brought no action.
records.limitations: Allegations by residents; the accused deny or did not respond; the executive officer's name is given only as 'Risil' Collected 2026-11-11 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 3823 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.
