records.titleEn: Illegal sand extraction continues in Pabna amid administration's silence, cropland lost to the Padma
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's site visit; statements from farmers, the Choratarapur union chairman, the accused Sujanagar chairman, the UNO and the police super
records.location: Bhaduriadangi area, Choratarapur union, Pabna Sadar upazila, Pabna
records.summary: Dhaka Times reported that at Bhaduriadangi in Choratarapur union, Pabna Sadar upazila, Pabna, sand is being extracted illegally from the Padma River with the connivance of an influential syndicate while the administration stays silent. The report says severe river erosion is consuming hundreds of bighas of farmers' cropland, and locals said that if this continues little cropland will be left. On a site visit, the reporter saw 15 to 20 dredgers working openly, and more than 100 trawlers carrying the sand to Pakshi and Sujanagar in Pabna, Pangsha and Kumarkhali in Kushtia, Rajbari and other places. Armed miscreants reportedly guard the operation and threaten anyone who protests with death. The report says the sand traders extract and sell sand worth Tk 30 to 40 lakh a day. Affected farmers alleged that Sujanagar upazila parishad chairman Shahinuzzaman Shahin and Dogachhi union chairman Ali Hasan of Pabna Sadar lead the extraction under the patronage of a controversial Pabna contractor. They also alleged that farmers who protested, including through a human chain with local representatives, have been held on false cases and harassed by police. Choratarapur union chairman Siddiqur Rahman Siddik said complaints to the local MP, deputy commissioner, superintendent of police, UNO and river police brought no remedy, and said some influential people led by Shahin are involved in the extraction. Shahin, who is also general secretary of the Pabna Sadar upazila Awami League, denied involvement and said no sand is being extracted at Choratarapur. Dogachhi chairman Ali Hasan could not be reached for comment. Pabna Sadar UNO Tahmida Akter said no approval for sand extraction has been given in the area and that action will be taken if complaints are received. Superintendent of Police Akbar Ali Munshi said the current agitation and violence prevents police from watching the sand mahal, but that he would consult the district administration, BIWTA and river police before acting.
records.limitations: Allegations by farmers and a local chairman; accused denies; Dogachhi chairman not reached; no independent figures for volume or land loss Collected 2026-11-12 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 3697 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.title: Sand mining in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta sinks homes, livelihoods and hopes
records.titleEn: Sand mining in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta sinks homes, livelihoods and hopes
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: Published Nov 22, 2023, 01:00 PM
records.location: Can Tho city and Hau Giang province, Mekong Delta, southern Vietnam
records.summary: AFP reports that shoreline erosion linked to sand mining and upstream hydropower dams threatens hundreds of thousands of people in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, with homes collapsing into the Hau river in Can Tho and Hau Giang. It cites a WWF report and a 2018 WWF-led Mekong River Commission study saying sediment could fall by up to 97 per cent by 2040. Government figures show at least 750km of riverbank and nearly 2,000 houses sank into rivers between 2016 and August 2023. Vietnam's Ministry of Transport says the delta needs 54 million cubic m of sand for six highways before 2025 and the river system can supply less than half. Mekong expert Nguyen Huu Thien says that at an extraction rate of 35 million to 55 million cubic m a year, sand would run out by 2035. State media report over US$470 million spent on 190 anti-erosion projects since 2016, and officials cite around 20,000 households needing resettlement, while WWF says half a million could lose homes. Alternatives such as sea sand or Cambodian imports are being debated, and projects have been delayed.
records.limitations: News report; figures are attributed to WWF, the MRC-linked study, ministries, and state media and are not independently verified here; no specific mining site data; Hau river is the only named river. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: শ্যামনগরে অবৈধভাবে বালু উত্তোলনের অভিযোগ
records.titleEn: Allegation of illegal sand extraction in Shyamnagar
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's calls with the dredger owner, local land officials, DoE officer and RDC; copy of approval letter; unnamed sources; environmentalist comment
records.location: Purakatla area, Buri Goalini union, Shyamnagar upazila, Satkhira
rivers: A river at Purakatla, Buri Goalini
records.summary: A BD24Live report published on 22 February 2023 alleges that sand is being illegally extracted by dredger machine from a river on about 3.5 acres of land at Purakatla (Porakatla) in Buri Goalini union, Shyamnagar upazila, Satkhira district, in an area the report describes as ecologically critical. The report does not name the river. Dredger owner Faruk Hossain said the owner of the firm M/S Ar-Rad Corporation is Sabuj Khan and that they were extracting with the Deputy Commissioner's approval. The approval copy he provided says the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Shyamnagar, and the Water Development Board recommended extraction by scientific dredging while maintaining environmental balance. Union assistant land officer Kamal Hossain said there was approval; when asked about the report on illegal extraction from an ecologically critical area, he reportedly said angrily that he had no time for stories and cut the call. Upazila Assistant Commissioner (Land) Md Asaduzzaman said the DC approved it on the basis of a Department of Environment clearance. Satkhira DoE officer Sardar Shafiqul Islam denied this, saying clearance is never given for extraction in ecologically critical areas and none was issued for Buri Goalini. Satkhira RDC Md Mohiuddin, whose signature is on the approval, said it was granted after reports from the Water Development Board and the AC (Land) found extraction suitable under scientific dredging. Several unnamed people involved alleged that, out of excess profit, Water Development Board and AC (Land) officials, together with some influential local people, concealed the area's ecologically critical status and reported that there was no problem with extraction. The report cites Sections 5 and 11 of the Balumahal and Soil Management Act 2010 (Act No. 62), which it says bar extraction of sand or soil from rivers or underground by pump or dredging, and bar extraction, transport and marketing from a balumahal without a lease. Jahangir Alam of Barsik said river sand extraction obstructs river flow, causes embankment erosion, damages fish habitats and food chains, and harms soil, water and biodiversity.

records.title: Mining the Mekong: Land and Livelihoods Lost to Cambodia’s Thirst for Sand
records.titleEn: Mining the Mekong: Land and Livelihoods Lost to Cambodia’s Thirst for Sand
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: Story August 29, 2022
records.location: Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, on the Mekong River, Cambodia; also the Bassac River
records.summary: Pulitzer Center story (supported by its Rainforest Investigations Network) reports that residents of Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, blame sand mining by politically connected companies for riverbank collapses on the Mekong that have cost them homes and fishing-based livelihoods. The Cambodian government, via Ung Dipola of the Ministry of Mines and Energy, denies that dredging causes erosion and says it helps stabilise the banks; University of Newcastle and University of Southampton researchers call this "a myth". According to the Ministry of Mines and Energy, Cambodia has 49 active licenses covering 2,320 hectares of the Mekong and Bassac rivers, and 11.7 million m3 of sand was extracted in 2020 and 11.5 million m3 in 2021, with 6.1 million m3 in the first six months of 2022. Dipola said only around 4% of the river is licensed for dredging. Hackney's research suggested extraction exceeded natural replenishment by almost five times in 2018 and by a factor of 16 in 2020. Echo-sounder surveys by Leyland and Darby found extraction scars routinely 5 m deep and one barge taking roughly 9,450 m3 in a day. The researchers warn that riverbed lowering could affect the Tonle Sap reversal of flow. The article also describes company ownership links to political elites, including Global Green Energy Development, Jin Ling Construction and Sophearoth Aphivath, and says the government has not released the environmental impact assessments.
records.limitations: The supplied article text is truncated and ends mid-sentence. Allegations about company links and the official's family ties are attributed to the reporting. Residents' causal claims are disputed by officials. No publisher datePublished metadata was supplied, so the date is taken from the body text. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.
records.reviewDetail: Automated editorial review passed; owner review pending

records.title: The untold environmental catastrophe that is being caused by continuous sand miningSand mining -- the silent killer of environment | International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD)
records.titleEn: The untold environmental catastrophe that is being caused by continuous sand mining: Sand mining -- the silent killer of environment
records.dateEvidence: Opinion piece based on the authors' reported visit to Netrokona, resident accounts, and the Sand Quarry and Soil Management Act, 2010
records.location: Durgapur Upazila, Netrokona district; national context
topics: Sand Quarry and Soil Management Act 2010
records.summary: In an opinion piece by Fatema Akhter and Dr Mizan R Khan of ICCCAD, originally published in Dhaka Tribune, the authors argue that illegal, indiscriminate and unscientific sand mining damages Bangladesh's ecosystems. They say illegal mining is an offence under the Sand Quarry and Soil Management Act, 2010, which prohibits quarrying within a kilometer of bridges, culverts, dams, barrages, embankments, highways, rail tracks, residential areas and other important structures. They say miners are leased a certain part of a river but in most cases go well beyond it, and that local monitoring is hardly present. Based on a recent visit to Netrokona, the authors describe the Someshwari river, which flows into Bangladesh through Durgapur Upazila, as close to extinction, so dry that one can walk over it. They report that mining has caused habitat loss, bank erosion, loss of fishing as a livelihood, depleted surface and groundwater, saline intrusion, deep gorges and landslides that occasionally kill local people, and noise and air pollution affecting Hajong, Mandi and other ethnic groups. Residents allege illicit mining is carried out with the cooperation of elected public leaders, and that sand is also used to fill wetlands before land-grabbing. The authors call for environmental impact assessments before authorizing mining, stronger laws, community monitoring, public awareness, an international framework and alternatives to sand. The article gives no volume, fine or revenue figures.
records.limitations: Opinion/advocacy; resident allegations not independently verified; republished from Dhaka Tribune; no quantitative data Collected 2026-11-15 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 8511 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.title: পদ্মা সেতুর নিচ থেকে অবৈধ বালু উত্তোলন
records.titleEn: Illegal sand extraction from beneath the Padma Bridge
records.dateEvidence: Reporter site visit on Thursday, the permit paper read by reporters, and statements from the bridge executive engineer, the River Research Institute official, the deputy commissioner, a resident and the contractor's representative.
records.location: Jajira end of the Padma Bridge, Shariatpur; Painpara char nearby
rivers: Padma River, beneath the 39th span of the Padma Bridge (Jajira end)
records.summary: NewsBangla reported from Shariatpur on 29 May 2021 (updated the same day) that sand was being lifted day and night from the Padma River beneath the 39th span of the Padma Bridge at the Jajira end, Shariatpur. Three dredging machines were being used by Khokon Construction and Engineering Limited, and one bulkhead (sand-carrying vessel) after another carried the sand away. The sand was going into land development for a government project, the Sheikh Hasina Tantpolli, being built on 120 acres across Shariatpur and Madaripur districts, where about 13.5 lakh cubic metres of sand is to be filled. The report said sand purchase in the project was budgeted at about Tk 23.60 crore (23 crore 60 lakh), yet the contractor was illegally extracting sand, using influence, to continue the work. The contractor claimed it had permission. The Padma Bridge authority and district administration said the firm was permitted only vessel movement through the bridge area, not sand extraction. Reporters who visited on Thursday read the two-page permit and found no mention of sand extraction. Supervisor Md. Jasim Uddin said he had no other paper and that one might be at the office. The report cited sections 4(kha) and (ga) of the Balumahal and Soil Management Act 2010, which bans sand extraction within one kilometre of bridges, culverts, embankments, roads, railway lines and other important structures. It said the unplanned extraction had caused river erosion at the neighbouring Painpara char, and 110 char families had submitted a written petition to the deputy commissioner against it. Resident Rahima Begum said dredgers cut day and night and erosion was destroying char farmland. Rezaul Karim, chief scientific officer of the Bangladesh River Research Institute, expressed concern and said extraction without a survey and design could harm the bridge. Padma Bridge executive engineer Dewan Abdul Kader said the Bangladesh Bridge Authority had given no permission for sand extraction and he did not know whether the contractor was extracting sand near the bridge. Syed Abul Bashar, Madaripur district Awami League vice-president, who works for the contractor, said that because there is no balumahal in the region they extract sand without royalty. Deputy Commissioner Md. Parvez Hasan said no one had been permitted to extract sand from the river, there is no balumahal in Shariatpur, and anyone doing so is acting completely illegally and would not be spared.
records.limitations: Allegations of illegal extraction; contractor disputes by claiming permission; the engineer says he does not know whether extraction occurs; page includes unrelated recommended stories that were ignored. Collected 2026-11-13 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 23007 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.summary: Bd24live reported that the administration ran a mobile court over illegal sand extraction from the Jamuna River and char areas at Bhuapur, Tangail. The report says the court imposed a fine of Tk 2.5 lakh (2 lakh 50 thousand), sentenced two people to 10 days' simple imprisonment each, and seized 19 trucks along with excavator earth-cutting machines (5 excavators). On Sunday (23 May), around noon, a Tangail District DB police team raided what the paper calls the long-running illegal sand ghat of 'Khoka' in the Jigatola section of the Jamuna in Bhuapur. Police detained two people, held five excavators used for extraction and 19 drum trucks used for sand transport, and informed the administration. Executive magistrate and upazila assistant commissioner (land) Abdullah Al Roni arrived around 4 pm. Two labourers, Moinuddin and Salam, were handed to police, and the trucks and excavators were left in the custody of Gabsara union UP member Abdus Salam. The court sentenced Moinuddin (Jigatola village) and Salam (Nikolara village) to 10 days' simple imprisonment each, and fined Ranju of Jigatola village Tk 2.5 lakh. Judge Roni said the court was run with help from Tangail DB police and local police. The article states that ghat owner Khoka, described as an influential sand grabber, and his associates remained out of reach and no one from that group was brought under the law. Note: the judge's quoted statement as printed says 5 trucks and 19 excavators, which conflicts with the report's own earlier figures of 5 excavators and 19 trucks.

records.titleEn: Intensifying saline water intrusion and drought in the Mekong Delta: From physical evidence to policy outlooks
records.authors: Ho Huu Loc, Doan Van Binh, Edward Park, Sangam Shrestha, Tran Duc Dung, Vu Hai Son, Nguyen Hoang Thu Truc, Nguyen Phuong Mai, Chris Seijger
records.dateEvidence: Sci Total Environ. 2021 Feb 25:757:143919. Epub 2020 Dec 3 Date supplied by Gemini; independent date verification is pending.
records.location: 11 gauge stations across the Vietnamese Mekong Delta
records.summary: Applying spectral analysis and rating-curve diagnostics to multi-decadal hourly-to-daily water-level and salinity records at 11 VMD stations, this study documents up to 66% tidal amplification and rating-curve slope shifts. records.limitations: Gauge-based spectral and rating-curve analyses capture aggregate channel deepening without isolating individual illegal mining pits. The study discusses combined drivers and does not isolate individual mining operations.

records.title: Tight regulation stressed in sand mining
records.titleEn: Tight regulation stressed in sand mining
records.dateEvidence: Report of webinar speeches by an academic, an economist, the planning minister and officials
records.location: National
records.summary: At a webinar titled 'Can River Sand Mining Be a Sustainable Business?', organised by Change Initiative and Oxfam Bangladesh on Thursday (the article is dated 3 December 2020), speakers said river sand mining is crucial for Bangladesh for its economic value and for maintaining river navigability, but must be organised, citing that in most cases sand is lifted illegally. The report names no specific river or site and treats the issue nationally. Keynote presenter Estiaque Bari of East West University said the construction sector was valued at $24 billion in the 2018-19 fiscal year, 7% of GDP, and that sand, a key construction ingredient, has maintained a 7% growth rate for the last five years. He said illegal lifting continues in different parts of the country despite a dedicated sand mining law, and that the government allows mining mainly to improve navigation and meet growing demand. Dr AK Enamul Haque of the Asian Center for Development stressed that lifting is important given the huge silt entering rivers each year, but must be legal, noted sand's wide use in land filling, and urged regulation to curb illegal and unwise lifting. Planning Minister Muhammad Abdul Mannan, chief guest, said he would convey the issue to policy makers and try to form a regulation to ensure legalised sand mining. National River Conservation Commission member Md Alauddin and Change Initiative executive director M Zakir Hossain Khan also spoke.
records.limitations: Speakers' statements and opinions; no site-specific data or independent verification Collected 2026-11-13 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 2832 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

records.location: Ghatabari area, Jalalpur union, Shahjadpur upazila, Sirajganj
records.summary: A Sirajganj correspondent's report said sand extraction on the Jamuna continues despite a mobile court having burned a dredger. In Ghatabari area of Jalalpur union, Shahjadpur upazila, Sirajganj, a local group has reportedly set up a dredger again after about a year, extracting sand and selling it nearby, and riverbank erosion has reportedly increased. The report said locals allege the group is threatening to kill those who obstruct it, and residents submitted a written complaint to the upazila executive officer (UNO). It says Khukni and Jalalpur unions in eastern Shahjadpur are already battered by Jamuna erosion, with at least several thousand houses lost to the river in the past 5 years. On 29 November of the previous year, a mobile court led by the UNO burned an illegal dredger. The report names Majnu Mia of Baghabari, Raju of Shreephaltala (who claims to be a union parishad secretary in Kazipur) and several people from Rupshi village as having started cutting sand with the dredger over about the past week. Rubel Bhuiyan of Rupshi village, who applied to the UNO on behalf of residents, said sand looters attacked and threatened him for working against illegal extraction. UNO Shah Mohammad Shamsuzzoha said illegal extraction will not be allowed anywhere in the upazila, that he had heard a dredger was operating at Ghatabari, and that strict action would be taken soon.
records.limitations: Allegations by residents and a complainant; named individuals are accused in the report, not independently verified; no extraction volumes given. records.summary: DBC News reported on 25 September 2020 that dredgers installed haphazardly for unplanned sand extraction from the Meghna River in the char areas of Raipura upazila, Narsingdi, were threatening riverside communities. According to the report, erosion appeared on the Meghna in Raipura from the start of the monsoon season and continued, swallowing hundreds of houses, and several villages in Paratali and Mirzachar unions were being lost to the river. Hundreds of homes, trees and crop land in several villages of Nabipur union in neighbouring Brahmanbaria district were also under threat. Locals alleged that the local administration was not monitoring the activity. Locals said the district administration had leased a balumahal in Purba Hossainnagar mouza, Chanpur union, to Joybangla Traders, but the lessees evaded the administration and set up dredgers in various villages of Paratali union, about three kilometres from the designated site, extracting sand from the Meghna bank areas and causing erosion. Deputy Commissioner Syeda Farhana Kaunain said that if the balumahal caused erosion it would be stopped if necessary. She said the lessees had been served a show-cause notice under the rules, their reply was not found acceptable, and the lease had therefore been cancelled. Residents demanded a halt to unplanned sand extraction and the construction of an embankment to protect the homes of lakhs of people and the crop land in the Raipura char areas.
records.limitations: Allegations by locals; no volumes or erosion measurements given Collected 2026-11-13 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 1601 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.title: Dredging projects bleed money as silt returns to rivers
records.titleEn: Dredging projects bleed money as silt returns to rivers
records.dateEvidence: IMED report as described by the newspaper; quotes from IMED Secretary and two water experts; BIWTA survey cited; photos of Padma dredging sites
records.location: National; Chowhali upazila, Sirajganj; Doarabazar upazila, Sunamganj; Madaripur and Gopalganj
rivers: Jamuna, Brahmaputra, Buriganga, Padma, Bhairob-Chatok route, Madaripur-Charmuguria-Tekerhat-Gopalganj route, Mongla-Pakshi route via Chandpur-Maoa-Goalanda
records.summary: The Business Standard reported (18 October 2019) that the planning ministry's Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) found irregularities in five river dredging projects worth about Tk5,000 crore, and suspects misuse of funds in 97 other ongoing projects worth Tk47,000 crore run by BIWTA, the Water Development Board and others. IMED said the projects proceeded without needed surveys and its calls to dump silt properly were mostly unheeded. In a six-year Jamuna dredging project that ended in 2016, silt was dumped on banks and farmland and monsoon rain washed it back into the river; three unions of Chowhali upazila, Sirajganj, went into the river. A follow-up project was allocated almost half the original project's sum. In a project to dredge 136km from the Jamuna-Brahmaputra junctions to the Buriganga, rivers silted up a year after the 2010 dredging; 40km was re-dredged in 2015 and silted up the next year. The Tk944 crore project was extended by six and a half years and its cost rose to Tk1,125 crore. In a Tk956 crore project for the Mongla port-Pakshi route via Chandpur-Maoa-Goalanda (460km, continuing until 2025, to carry Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant equipment), silt was dumped on banks and the same places were dredged repeatedly; IMED recommended proper fencing and dumping away from banks. In a capital dredging project on 53 inland waterway routes, 27 percent of silt was dumped on agricultural land and 29 percent on river banks; dredging about 2,500km at around Tk2,000 crore brought no positive outcome, per the report. Erosion hit Doarabazar upazila, Sunamganj, due to a design fault in the Bhairob-Chatok dredging project. On the 92km Madaripur-Charmuguria-Tekerhat-Gopalganj route, 23 percent of silt has already returned. IMED recommended pre-dredging surveys in 2011. IMED Secretary Abul Mansur Mohammad Faizullah said IMED can only recommend and punishment rests with ministries. Experts Ainun Nishat and AKM Saiful Islam said siltation is continuous and urged planned, river-specific dredging and maintenance dredging. A BIWTA survey says waterways spanned 84,000km in monsoon and 52,000km in dry season in 1962-67, now 6,000km and 3,800km.

records.summary: UNB reported on 1 September 2019 that sand is being extracted illegally from the Dudhkumar River at Nurani Para near Jatrapur Bazar, Kurigram Sadar upazila, Kurigram, leaving 120 families under threat of riverbank erosion. Locals said a syndicate, in connivance with Upazila Parishad man Shafiqul Islam, has been extracting sand for about two weeks, using a dredger and a pipe placed in the river, and that accidents happen daily. Locals said silt at the mouth of the Brahmaputra has blocked other entry to Jatrapur Bazar, so the Dudhkumar is the only river route; more than 300 char inhabitants use it to reach Nageshwari, Ulipur, Roumari, Chilmari and Rajibpur upazilas. Last year the Water Development Board (WDB) spent Tk 3 crore on geo-sandbag embankments and piling at Nurani and Farazi Para against erosion, and residents said the dredger operates in the same area. They said written complaints went to the Deputy Commissioner, Upazila Parishad Chairman, UNO, WDB and Kurigram Press Club. Local journalists said that after Shafiqul Islam visited on 21 August, ostensibly to have the pipe removed, the dredger ran through the night; the UNB correspondent found it operating on 26 and 29 August. Residents said the sand is for a four-storey building at Chakenda Khanpara High School; sand traders declined to speak on record, saying ruling party activists and influential school committee people direct the extraction. Boatmen said ferrying takes an extra 30-40 minutes. Jatrapur Union Chairman Ayub Ali Sarkar said the machine was removed once after protests but reinstalled on the opposite bank. Kurigram Sadar UNO Nilufa Yasmin said her men told her the dredger had been removed and asked whom to believe.

records.title: Illegal sand lifting wreaks havoc along Brahmaputra
records.titleEn: Illegal sand lifting wreaks havoc along Brahmaputra
records.dateEvidence: Unnamed sources and villagers quoted; named farmers; statement from the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General); a photo caption of sand lifting at Char Jatharthapur.
records.location: Sonkanda to Narundi stretch and Char Jatharthapur Ujanpara village, Jamalpur Sadar upazila, Jamalpur
records.summary: The Independent's Jamalpur correspondent reported that unabated sand lifting in the Brahmaputra River has damaged agricultural land and houses in Jamalpur Sadar upazila, Jamalpur. Sources said illegal gangs have set up as many as 11 dragging machines along the river from Sonkanda to Narundi. They said each machine lifted around 30,000 cubic feet of sand a day, so over 3 lakh cubic feet was being lost daily. A source said the lifters flout sustainable limits and scoop sand at night, and that the gangs make money while depriving the government of revenue. Farmer Akram Hossain of Char Jatharthapur Ujanpara village complained that one bigha of his crop field was damaged; Ashraful Islam, Sohag Miah and Abdul Motaleb echoed the complaint. They said the syndicates are influential and villagers fear confronting them. Sources said the sand was being used to fill the side of a private power plant at Char Jatharthapur Ujanpara, and that the mining has turned the river's flow northward, raising the prospect of large-scale erosion at Char Jatharthapur Ujanpara, Bhatipara and adjacent villages in the next rainy season. Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Md Rasel Sabrin said sand lifting is prohibited in the area because a case is pending in the High Court, that no permission has been given, and that mobile courts and legal action would follow.
records.limitations: Figures and allegations come from unnamed sources and villagers; no independent measurement reported. Collected 2026-11-14 by GitHub Actions (firecrawl read, 7037 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed.

Some participants proposed a total ban, while others said only reduced extraction is feasible now because of high construction demand and no substitutes.

records.titleEn: A grand festival of sand lifting, fear of collapse of embankment worth a hundred crore taka
records.dateEvidence: Reporter's site visit, local residents, former union chairman, WDB engineer, UNO and police OC quoted; named alleged operator quoted
records.location: Chinirpatal, Sathalia, Haldia and Beragram areas, Saghata upazila, Gaibandha
rivers: Jamuna River (also Katakhali river sites such as Trimohoni Ghat named in the report)
records.summary: Bdnews24's Gaibandha correspondent reported that continuous sand extraction from the Jamuna River has put the Saghata Bazar protection project embankment in Gaibandha at risk of collapse. Sand has long been lifted with shallow machines along the riverbank at Chinirpatal, Sathalia, Haldia and Beragram in Saghata upazila. The Gaibandha Water Development Board (WDB) said the project to protect Saghata Bazar and adjoining areas from Jamuna erosion was taken up in 2011 at a cost of Tk 135 crore, and the work finished in June 2016. On a Friday-morning site visit the reporter saw five shallow machines in a row at Chinirpatal pumping sand through pipes into piles on the bank, from which contractors from Saghata and other areas buy it by tractor. Locals said that for several months 15 shallow machines have been working day and night at Chinirpatal, Sathalia, Haldia and Beragram. A tractor load sells for Tk 1,000 to 1,200, and 70 to 80 tractor loads are reportedly lifted daily from each area. The report said Zahurul Islam, former Saghata upazila Chhatra League president, and his people extract and sell sand year-round with shallow machines at sites on the Katakhali river (Trimohoni Ghat, the area near Ramnagar Adarsha Gram, Satitala Ghat, Iliyas Ghat, Shankarganj Ghat) and on the Jamuna (Gobindi, Haldia, Hasilkandi, Dakshin Ulya/Baromataid). Chinirpatal traders Mojahar Ali (55) and Chhadrul Mia (50) said they had lost their homesteads four times to the Jamuna and that erosion had stopped for the past two years because of the project, but they feared the next flood would erode Saghata Bazar, the thana complex, the upazila health complex, other government and private installations and several villages. Former Saghata union council chairman A K M Fazlul Haque said the Tk 135 crore could be lost and about 20 villages could be swallowed by the river, and alleged that repeated complaints to the upazila administration brought no remedy. Zahurul Islam said the sand is lifted after managing local notables and the administration. Upazila executive officer Ujjal Kumar Ghosh said several complaints had been received and police asked to act. WDB sub-divisional engineer Chandra Shekhar said a general diary (GD) was filed at Saghata police station and a request made to remove the machines quickly. Saghata OC Mostafizur Rahman said the WDB's GD lacked names and addresses, but the process of taking action was under way.
records.limitations: Allegations and fears by residents and a former chairman; collapse risk is a projection; figures on machines and daily loads are locals' accounts Collected 2026-11-13 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 3319 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

The editorial argues that local politicians of the current regime are profiteering unlawfully, says the authorities have turned a blind eye, and urges the government to act.

Unnamed rivers in Sarishabari, Islampur and Madarganj
records.summary: Dhaka Times reported that illegal sand extraction is under way at about 50 points on various rivers, from the Jamalpur town ferry ghat to Piarpur in Sadar upazila and in Sarishabari, Islampur and Madarganj upazilas, Jamalpur. The paper said a locally influential group, operating as a syndicate, uses dredgers to lift sand from sand mahals and rivers, threatening farmland and costing the government revenue, while local administration appeared indifferent. According to the report, extraction covers a 25-kilometre stretch of the Brahmaputra through Naobhanga and Roshidpur (Jamalpur municipal area) and Ferighat, Chhonkanda, Charjothartthopur, Nandina, Narundi and Piarpur in Sadar upazila. Influential contractors also reportedly use river sand for several large roads and bridge approach roads. It said sand has been taken illegally without lease for about 11 years from several sand mahals including Chhonkanda and Charjothartthopur, and that the administration cannot act against the syndicate, so the government loses crores of taka in revenue each year. Dredging reportedly makes surrounding soil subside and banks collapse, and land used for extraction and sand storage damages farmland. Syndicate members could not be reached; dredger owners and those in charge claimed they had permission from local leaders and contractors but would not name them. Deputy Commissioner Shahabuddin Khan said he was aware, that several sand extraction machines had been seized and fines imposed, and that efforts continue. He said leasing of several sand mahals is halted because of court cases, which the administration is trying to resolve.

Transport problems have slowed sales: daily production is 3,500 tonnes while sales are 2,000 tonnes. A site visit found no space left in the yard. Managing Director Abul Bashar of Petrobangla's Madhyapara Granite Mining Company Ltd said production is proceeding normally as per target and the sales slowdown will pass quickly. The report says national demand is estimated at 8 million (80 lakh) tonnes a year, so production could be raised. Madhyapara stone is marketed nationwide through 21 dealers and used in roads, railways and government infrastructure. Store manager Syed Rafizul Islam said the stone is of high quality, better than India's Pakur grade, and that the government has directed its use; use in the Padma Bridge has also been announced. Several company sources said government project authorities are still not using it much. The contractor Germania Trest Consortium (GTC) has been extracting stone at Madhyapara since 2013 and said it will start expansion work soon, though demand must rise.

records.location: Makueni County
records.summary: The Makueni County Sand Conservation and Utilization Act, 2015 creates the Makueni County Sand Conservation and Utilization Authority, sub-county committees and sand resource user associations, and licenses sand harvesters and dealers. It allows harvesting and transport only between 6am and 6pm, with offenders liable to two years' imprisonment or a fine of 200,000 shillings or both. Riverbed harvesting must retain a sand reserve for water retention, is barred on riverbanks, and is banned within one hundred metres of infrastructure such as bridges. Sand revenue is split 50% to a conservation fund, 25% to the Authority, 20% to the county government and 5% to the local community.

records.title: Sand and Soil Management Act, 2010 (Act No. 62 of 2010).
records.titleEn: Sand and Soil Management Act, 2010 (Act No. 62 of 2010).
records.dateEvidence: FAOLEX database summary of the statute text
records.location: National
records.summary: This record describes the Sand and Soil Management Act, 2010 (Act No. 62 of 2010) of Bangladesh, which provides for the grant of leases for mining sand and soil and for suppressing illegal mining activities. It is national legislation, and the text names no river or specific extraction site. Section 4 prohibits sand and soil extraction from any environmentally sensitive area, from river banks damaged by dredging, from areas near a reservoir or embankment, or where there is a possibility of environmental damage. Section 5 restricts extraction by pumping or dredging. Section 6 makes the Ministry of Land the sole authority for granting leases or for marketing sand or soil lifted by government authority. Section 10 lays down the procedure for granting balumahal leases, and Section 15 provides for offences and penalties.
records.limitations: Summary of the Act by FAOLEX, not the full statutory text; no penalty amounts stated; only the year 2010 is given. Collected 2026-11-18 by GitHub Actions (tinyfish read, 734 characters); summaries by claude-sonnet-5-5; editorial review passed after revision.

records.titleEn: Nation-wide mapping shows linkages between sand mining activities, human land use, and hydrology in Rwanda
records.publisher: One Earth (Cell Press), via University of Copenhagen Research Portal
records.authors: Ke Huang, Lars Lonsmann Iversen, Rasmus Fensholt, Dimitri Gominski, Martin Brandt, Maurice Mugabowindekwe, Niels Strange, Mette Bendixen
records.dateEvidence: No publication date found on the source page
records.location: National scope
records.summary: This peer-reviewed study applied deep learning to high-resolution aerial imagery to map sand extraction across Rwanda. It reports that mining sites increased by 18% to 3,751 between 2008 and 2023, that sites are spatially linked to river valleys and urban development at sub-watershed level, and that expansion over the past decade often encroached into agricultural areas. The authors present the method as a scalable way to monitor sand extraction and its environmental implications.

records.title: Everything comes from something: A geographic photo analysis of sand extraction and usage in Rwanda’s rapidly growing economy
records.titleEn: Everything comes from something: A geographic photo analysis of sand extraction and usage in Rwanda's rapidly growing economy
records.dateEvidence: No publication date found on the source page
records.location: Nyabugogo River near Kigali; Rusine River; a tributary of the river spelled 'Mukuwunga' on the Northern-Western Province border; Rutongo Mines area
records.summary: A photo essay by McGill University geographer Mette Bendixen, based on fieldwork photos from June 2023 and 2024, documents artisanal sand extraction in Rwanda. On the Nyabugogo River near Kigali, men ranging from teenagers to their 40s stand hip-deep to dig sand from the riverbed, stockpiling it on platforms for dump trucks; riverbank erosion and collapse are described as common. On the Rusine River women crush stone while only men extract sand, and sand bags carried on the head weigh over 30 kilos. The author argues national housing plans omit sand, gravel and crushed stone.
records.limitations: Photo essay rather than a quantitative study; no publication date is printed on the page (DOI suggests 2025). The essay spells Nyabugogo as Nyabogogo and names a tributary of a 'Mukuwunga' River (possibly the Mukungwa, not tagged); districts are not named. English translation of the headline awaits native-language review.
